extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, policymakers, and advocates concerned with free-speech and liberty principles
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and principles for assessing when thought, speech, publication, association, and personal conduct should be protected or may be legitimately restricted by society or government. Grounded in the harm principle, corrigibility of human judgment, and historical examples of persecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of conscience and thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The inward domain of consciousness: liberty of conscience in the most comprehensive sense; liberty of thought and feeling; absolute freedom of opinion and sentiment on all subjects, practical or speculative, scientific, moral, or theological.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is treated as the first and foundational liberty — the private mental sphere that must be free. The text insists on 'absolute freedom of opinion and sentiment' as the starting point for other liberties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of expression and publication as practically inseparable from liberty of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The liberty of expressing and publishing opinions is almost of as much importance as the liberty of thought itself, and, resting in great part on the same reasons, is practically inseparable from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because expression is how thought affects society and can be tested, restrictions on publication are treated as equivalent in gravity to restrictions on thought. Historical notes (e.g. press prosecutions of 1858) illustrate consequences of governmental interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of tastes, pursuits, and personal conduct (harm-limited)
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty of tastes and pursuits; of framing the plan of our life to suit our own character; of doing as we like, subject to such consequences as may follow: without impediment from our fellow-creatures, so long as what we do does not harm them, even though they should think our conduct foolish, perverse, or wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal actions and lifestyles should be free unless they harm others. The threshold for restriction is harm to others rather than mere disapproval or perceived foolishness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of association (combination) under non-harm constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: From this liberty of each individual follows the liberty, within the same limits, of combination among individuals; freedom to unite for any purpose not involving harm to others: the persons combining being supposed to be of full age, and not forced or deceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedom to join and act collectively is protected so long as participants are adults and voluntary, and the purpose does not harm others. Coercion or deception of participants undermines legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: A society that does not respect these liberties is not free
rubrics_metrics.description: No society in which these liberties are not, on the whole, respected, is free, whatever may be its form of government; and none is completely free in which they do not exist absolute and unqualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedom is defined functionally by the presence of these liberties; qualified or partial guarantees do not amount to true freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency of society and institutions to overreach — need for moral vigilance
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an increasing inclination to stretch unduly the powers of society over the individual, both by the force of opinion and even by that of legislation; and as the tendency of all the changes taking place in the world is to strengthen society, and diminish the power of the individual, this encroachment is not likely to disappear unless a strong barrier of moral conviction is raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy evaluation should account for the social and legislative pressures to expand control; advocates and institutions must cultivate moral conviction to resist unjust encroachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silencing opinions assumes infallibility and is therefore illegitimate
rubrics_metrics.description: To refuse a hearing to an opinion, because [we] are sure that it is false, is to assume that their certainty is the same thing as absolute certainty. All silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A core evaluative rule: prohibition of speech on the ground that it is false is illegitimate because it presumes the authority to decide truth for all. This undercuts any justification that relies on the decision-makers' alleged certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silencing is a collective robbery (loss to present and posterity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The peculiar evil of silencing the expression of an opinion is, that it is robbing the human race; posterity as well as the existing generation; those who dissent from the opinion, still more than those who hold it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing restrictions, weigh the loss to public knowledge and future generations: if an opinion is right, suppression prevents truth; if wrong, suppression deprives others of the benefit of its refutation and of clearer perception of truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion is necessary for corrigibility and for justified action
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be discussion, to show how experience is to be interpreted. Wrong opinions and practices gradually yield to fact and argument: but facts and arguments... must be brought before [the mind]. The whole strength and value of human judgment... is that it can be set right when it is wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies that block open debate remove the essential mechanism by which human judgment is corrected. Decision-making and credible action require exposure to contestation; suppressed views cannot be properly tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness of belief requires invitation to challenge (devil's advocate principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The beliefs which we have most warrant for, have no safeguard to rest on, but a standing invitation to the whole world to prove them unfounded... The holiest of men... cannot be admitted to posthumous honours, until all that the devil could say against him is known and weighed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional and social processes should institutionalize challenge (e.g., adversarial testing) to make beliefs reliable. Lack of such challenge is a sign that confidence in a belief is unwarranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility cannot justify suppression without contestation of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The usefulness of an opinion is itself matter of opinion... There is the same need of an infallible judge of opinions to decide an opinion to be noxious, as to decide it to be false, unless the opinion condemned has full opportunity of defending itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments that certain beliefs must be legally protected because they are useful are invalid unless open debate has tested both their truth and their utility. 'Utility' cannot be invoked as a one-sided justification for prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular danger of forbidding discussion of moral or religious doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not the feeling sure of a doctrine... which I call an assumption of infallibility. It is the undertaking to decide that question for others, without allowing them to hear what can be said on the contrary side... And so far from the assumption being less objectionable because the opinion is called immoral or impious, this is the case of all others in which it is most fatal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suppressing debate about moral or religious doctrines is especially dangerous because history shows that such suppressions often silence deeply valuable truths (examples: Socrates, Christ) and lead to grave injustices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech may be punishable only when linked to an overt act (incipiency/connection standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The instigation to [tyrannicide] may be a proper subject of punishment, but only if an overt act has followed, and at least a probable connexion can be established between the act and the instigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This articulates an early incitement standard: punishments for speech require an overt act and a probable causal link. Mere advocacy of a doctrine (however immoral) is not by itself sufficient ground for criminal penalty without a likely connection to actionable harm.
